title: Join Us
text:
Open positions

PhD positions — start September 2027
We are looking for PhD students to work on underwater radiated noise from ships, propellers and cavitation noise, noise and vibration on board, ice-induced vibration of hulls and shaftlines, and noise control by design, including viscoelastic damping materials, sound insulation and the acoustic design of spaces on board, acoustic black holes and metamaterials. Projects range from numerical modelling and data analysis to laboratory experiments and full-scale measurements at sea. Not every project involves going to sea: we discuss with each student the balance between numerical, laboratory and field work that suits them. Positions are funded for four years, with a competitive stipend.


Master’s students and postdoctoral fellows
We occasionally have openings. Strong candidates with their own funding (for example NSERC, Mitacs or scholarships from their home country) are always welcome to get in touch.


Undergraduate students
Memorial students interested in co-op work terms or honours projects can email us at any time.



Members of the lab on deck during sea trials off Newfoundland, November 2025. Click to enlarge.

title: Join Us
text:
Who we’re looking for

A degree in naval architecture, mechanical, ocean or acoustical engineering, physics, mathematics or a related field
Solid foundations in mathematics and mechanics or physics. No previous experience in acoustics or vibration is needed: most of our students learn it here
Some programming experience, in any language (for example Python, MATLAB, C/C++ or Fortran)
For projects with fieldwork, willingness to spend time on board working vessels
Good communication skills in English, written and spoken
Curiosity for new knowledge, motivation for research and a willingness to learn subjects outside your own training

Experience with numerical modelling (for example finite element methods), laboratory testing or field measurements is an asset, not a requirement. We value different backgrounds: our students have come from engineering, physics and mathematics, and they learn from each other.

title: Join Us
text:
How to apply
Email lmoro [at] mun.ca with the subject line “PhD application – [your name]” and attach, as a single PDF:

A CV, including publications if any
Transcripts of your degrees (unofficial copies are fine)
A short statement (one page at most) on which of our research themes interests you and why

We read every application but can reply only to shortlisted candidates. Successful candidates will also apply formally through Memorial’s School of Graduate Studies, and must meet its admission requirements, including the English proficiency requirements for applicants whose previous degrees were not taught in English.

title: Join Us
text:
Living in St. John’s



Photo: Memorial University


St. John’s is the capital of Newfoundland and Labrador, a small city of about 250,000 people in the wider area, on the Atlantic coast. The campus is close to downtown and a short drive from the airport, with direct flights to Toronto, Montreal, Halifax and, in season, Europe.

Housing. Most graduate students rent off campus, close to the university. Memorial also has graduate residences on campus, including family units.
Outdoors. The East Coast Trail, Signal Hill and Cape Spear are on the city’s doorstep, and you can watch icebergs and whales in spring and summer.
Climate. Winters are milder than in most of Canada but long, windy and snowy, and spring can be foggy. Good rain gear matters more than a heavy parka.
Community. Memorial has a large international graduate community, and its Internationalization Office helps new students with permits, health coverage and settling in.

title: Facilities & Tools
text:
Underwater acoustics

Hydrophones: Ocean Sonics icListen smart hydrophones (24-bit, up to 200 kHz), including self-recording units, and Turbulence Research hydrophones with autonomous recorders.
Hydrophone buoy system: icListen hydrophones on an Ocean Sonics drifting buoy with radio telemetry, so the system can be monitored during measurements. Developed with Ocean Sonics in 2021.
Moorings: a single hydrophone or a vertical array configured to ISO 17208, with OpenSeas subsurface buoys and floats, temperature loggers along the line, and acoustic releases to recover the moorings.
Ocean gliders: we fitted a passive acoustic monitoring system to a Slocum glider of Memorial’s fleet, operated by the Autonomous Ocean Systems Centre (AOSCENT), to measure ship-radiated noise and map the sound-speed profile of the water column.

title: Facilities & Tools
text:
Vibration and structural dynamics

Accelerometers: more than 25 PCB Piezotronics uniaxial and triaxial ICP accelerometers.
Modal testing: an instrumented impact hammer and a PCB force sensor, and two The Modal Shop electrodynamic shakers with power amplifiers.
Shaftline measurements: strain-gauge rosettes with wireless LORD MicroStrain telemetry to measure shaft torque and torsional vibration on rotating shafts, and Brüel & Kjær laser tachometers for shaft speed. This is the system we use on board icebreakers to record ice–propeller interaction loads.

title: Facilities & Tools
text:
Airborne noise and occupational exposure

Sound level meter: Larson Davis SoundAdvisor 831C, with calibrator and measurement microphones.
Noise dosimeters: six Brüel & Kjær Type 4448 personal noise dosimeters for crew exposure surveys.
Sound source: omnidirectional dodecahedron source with amplifier, for room acoustics and sound insulation measurements.
Hearing protection kit: earplugs and earmuffs of different types, to study protection in noisy workplaces.

title: Facilities & Tools
text:
Data acquisition

National Instruments CompactDAQ systems (up to 8-slot chassis, 24-bit sound and vibration modules) and NI FieldDAQ rugged units for measurements at sea, with ruggedized laptops for field work.

title: Facilities & Tools
text:
Numerical modelling

MSC Nastran and the MSC Software suite: finite element models of ship structures for modal, forced-response and structure-borne noise analysis.
COMSOL Multiphysics: coupled structural-acoustic analysis with the finite element and boundary element methods, and ray tracing for sound propagation.
Statistical energy analysis (SEA): models of airborne and structure-borne noise transmission between the spaces of a ship, to predict noise levels on board and test noise control treatments at the design stage.
LS-DYNA: transient and impact analysis, including ice–structure interaction.
ANSYS: finite element and multiphysics analysis.
In-house codes in MATLAB and Python for signal processing, source-level estimation, propagation loss modelling, torsional vibration of shaftlines and uncertainty analysis.

title: Facilities & Tools
text:
Software

Shafting torsional vibration tool: our codes for the torsional vibration analysis of propulsion shaftlines, including ice–propeller interaction loads, developed over several projects with ABS.

title: Facilities & Tools
text:
Partner facilities

Towing tank, Memorial University: model-scale tests of propeller-induced hull pressures and vibration, and of underwater noise from propellers.
NRC Ocean, Coastal and River Engineering (OCRE), St. John’s: towing tank and cavitation tunnel. We are working with NRC to upgrade the cavitation tunnel to measure propeller noise.
SMART laboratory (Smart Materials Additive-manufacturing Research Technologies), Memorial University, led by Dr. Ahmed Elruby: metal additive manufacturing of acoustic black holes and propeller models, with mechanical and non-destructive testing.
ShipNVL – Ship Noise & Vibration Laboratory, University of Trieste (Italy): our long-standing partner lab, with joint projects, co-supervised students and shared experimental work on acoustic black holes and metamaterials.

title: Research
text:
Future Ocean and Coastal Infrastructures (FOCI)
From 2020 to 2026 Dr. Moro co-led FOCI with Dr. Paul Foley: a transdisciplinary research program on the infrastructures that safe, sustainable and inclusive coastal communities and ocean industries in Atlantic Canada depend on.
FOCI brought together 65 researchers and 89 partners from engineering, the natural and social sciences and the arts, and trained 81 students and early-career researchers. Its results went beyond academic papers, to a documentary film, a theatre piece and musical compositions. Within FOCI, we worked with colleagues in the Department of Ocean and Naval Architectural Engineering on design for the safety and sustainability of fishing vessels: on-board noise, stability, and a lower carbon footprint. FOCI also co-funded our 2025 Arctic measurement campaign aboard CCGS Henry Larsen.
Visit the FOCI website → fociresearch.ca

Projects

title: Research
section: Noise and vibration control by design
text:
Noise and vibration control by design
Engines, propellers and machinery excite the ship’s structure. The resulting vibration can harm comfort, equipment and the structure itself, and it is radiated as noise on board and into the sea. We design, model and test ways to control it: at the source, along the paths it travels through the structure, and in the spaces where people live and work.
Our topics include resilient mounts for marine engines, structure-borne transmission paths, viscoelastic materials and damping treatments, sound insulation of decks and bulkheads (floating floors, double-leaf panels and damped linings), the acoustic design of cabins and crew spaces, and acoustic black holes and metamaterials designed to work on a real hull in water. Most of this work moves from numerical simulation to laboratory testing. It builds on research begun at the Ship Noise & Vibration Laboratory (ShipNVL) of the University of Trieste, our partner lab.

Projects

2026–2032 · Passive control of structure-borne noise from marine engines using acoustic black holes (NSERC Discovery Grant)
2016–2024 · Prediction of structure-borne noise generated by reciprocating machines on board ships (NSERC Discovery Grant)
2016–2019 · Design solutions to mitigate noise and vibration on fishing vessels (Research and Development Corporation NL)

title: Research
text:
Underwater radiated noise from ships
Shipping is the main source of human-made noise in the ocean. We study how ships radiate noise, how to predict it and how reliably it can be measured.
On the computational side, we develop tools to predict the noise radiated by ships and statistical prediction models built from a large dataset of vessels. On the measurement side, we work on shallow-water procedures (ISO 17208-3) and on the uncertainty of source-level estimates, using a buoy-mounted hydrophone system with radio monitoring that we developed with Ocean Sonics.
Our Arctic work is part of Project 2.4, Noise Reduction, of the Clean Arctic Shipping Initiative, carried out in partnership with ICC Canada and Makivvik.

Projects

2024–2031 · Clean Arctic Shipping Initiative, Project 2.4 Noise Reduction (Canada First Research Excellence Fund)
2021–2024 · Validation of underwater radiated noise modelling via ship-specific measurements (Transport Canada)
2022–2023 · Baseline assessment of underwater radiated noise from shipping in Placentia Bay (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)

title: Research
text:
Ocean gliders and autonomous monitoring
Autonomous underwater gliders can stay at sea for weeks, collecting data far from any ship. We develop methods to measure the underwater noise radiated by passing ships with gliders, including how to account for the glider’s own self-noise and the uncertainty of the measurements.
With the University of Bologna, we are also developing a glider-based device and sampling strategy to monitor nano- and microplastics in seawater. This collaboration received the Canada–Italy Innovation Award in 2022.

Projects

2023–2026 · Sampling nano-plastics with an ocean glider, with the University of Bologna (Memorial University)
2018–2023 · Monitoring underwater noise from ships with autonomous gliders (Ocean Frontier Institute)

title: Research
text:
Noise and vibration on board
Seafarers and fish harvesters live and work next to engines, propellers and machinery for weeks at a time. We assess noise and vibration exposure on fishing vessels, at aquaculture sites and on research and Coast Guard ships. We measure personal exposures over full work shifts, map noise levels across vessels and facilities, identify the machinery and tasks that drive exposure, and recommend hearing protection suited to each task. We also study how crews perceive and manage that exposure.
We also develop computational tools, including statistical energy analysis models, to predict noise levels on board at the design stage and to find the dominant transmission paths, so that exposure can be reduced before a ship is built.

Projects

2018–2023 · Noise exposure of fish harvesters on large offshore fishing vessels (Ocean Frontier Institute, Module I, with SafetyNet)
2017–2024 · Noise exposure of aquaculture workers and solutions to reduce it (Ocean Frontier Institute, Module M, with SafetyNet)
2016–2019 · Improving fishing safety in Newfoundland and Labrador (Mitacs)

title: Research
text:
Ice-induced propeller shaft vibration
When a propeller hits ice, the shaft line receives sudden torque peaks that can overload the propulsion system. This work is about the safety and reliability of propulsion machinery on ice-going ships.
We model the torsional vibration of shaft lines with lumped-parameter and finite element methods, measure the shaft-line response on icebreakers in operation, and use the measurements to estimate the loads from ice–propeller interaction. Our torsional vibration codes support the design and classification of ice-class shafting.

Projects

2016–2024 · Ice-induced propeller shaft transient torsional vibration and on-board noise, Phases 1–3 (American Bureau of Shipping; Phase 3 with InnovateNL)

title: Research
text:
Ice-induced hull vibration
Ice impacts on the hull, and vibration transmitted from the propeller and shaft line, make the hull vibrate. This affects comfort on board, the performance of equipment and the fatigue life of the structure.
We model ice-induced hull vibration and the way vibration travels from the shaft line into the hull, and we validate the models with full-scale measurements from icebreakers in operation. We have also worked on models of dynamic ice–structure interaction.

Projects

2023–2025 · Safe operation of light ice class ships in Arctic waters (American Bureau of Shipping, Mitacs)
2018–2022 · Ship design and operation for harsh environments (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador)

title: Research
text:
Propellers and cavitation noise
The propeller is often the loudest source on a ship, and in ice it also carries the highest loads. Our newest line of work brings these two problems together.
We have measured the noise and vibration of model propellers in a towing tank. With the National Research Council of Canada, we are now upgrading a cavitation tunnel to measure propeller noise, and with Memorial’s additive manufacturing laboratory we are 3D-printing metal propellers to test new designs quickly.

Projects

2024–2029 · Smart Materials Additive-manufacturing Research Technologies, SMART (Energy Research and Development NL)
2018–2024 · Prediction of propeller-induced noise and hull vibration, PINOV (Transport Canada, National Research Council, InnovateNL)

title: Research
text:
Beyond ships
The same methods apply elsewhere. With orthopedic surgeons at Memorial, we are studying why operating rooms are so noisy and how to reduce it.

Projects

2026–2027 · Mitigating noise exposure in the orthopaedic operating room (Newfoundland and Labrador Health Research Fund)
